activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Brackets are cleared with the distributive property before solving: 3(x + 2) becomes 3x + 6, because the 3 multiplies both terms inside.
story:
Alex had been at the community centre for forty minutes, and his stack of math homework had dwindled from six problems to one.

The last problem was 3(x + 2) = 15, and it was winning.

He slumped lower at the table in the corner of the games room. Across from him, Talia was doing a puzzle, and Charleigh was supposedly doing homework too, though her page was mostly a drawing of a dragon.

"Any chance that's a two-minute problem?" Talia asked, without looking up.

"It's a trap problem. There's an x in there, but it's hiding behind brackets."

Charleigh leaned over. "Just do the thing where you divide both sides. Fifteen divided by three is five."

So Alex divided both sides by 3 and wrote x + 2 = 5, then subtracted 2 from both sides and got x = 3. He sat back, feeling extremely competent for about four seconds, until he tried checking it. Three times three plus two was eleven. The right side said fifteen. He read it again. Eleven did not equal fifteen, and no amount of staring made it equal fifteen.

"Great," he said. "Now the trap has trapped me."

Talia abandoned her puzzle. Charleigh put down her dragon. Alex erased the whole middle of the page, which was one of the more satisfying things he had done all week.

"Okay," he said. "The three outside the brackets has to go somewhere. When I divided, I only got rid of it for the x. But there's a two in there too." He wrote 3x + 6 = 15, the way he thought it should look if the three multiplied everything, and the way Talia's older sister had once scribbled on the whiteboard in this very room. Then he subtracted 6 from both sides. 3x = 9. Divide both sides by 3. x = 3. He checked it: three times three plus six was fifteen. He checked it again, because he did not trust the number 3 after what it had done to him.

"That's the same answer," Charleigh pointed out. "Three. You just took the long road."

"It's not the same, because the first one was a lie." He copied the step into his notes in his most careful handwriting: 3(x + 2) becomes 3x + 6, because the 3 multiplies both terms inside. Then, under it: brackets first, then both sides.

Ms. Cheung came by with the sign-in clipboard, glanced at his page, and nodded once, which was the closest thing to a standing ovation she ever gave anyone.

"One problem left, then the gym's open till eight," she said.

Alex looked at his notebook, then at the door. "Talia, you multiply both terms too, right? Tell me it's not just me."

"It's not just you," she said, and put the puzzle back in the box.

activity: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
knowledge_domain: to cook rice, a curry and flatbread so they are all ready at the same time
fact: When cooking several dishes for one meal, start with the one that takes longest and plan backward from the time you want to eat.
story:
Jake stood at the counter with three recipes spread out in front of him and a pencil behind his ear. Precious and Chelsea were coming over at seven o'clock for the dinner he had promised them, and he was cooking curry, rice, and flatbread, all from scratch, for the first time. The curry needed forty minutes. The rice needed twenty. The flatbread needed ten, plus rolling time. He stared at the numbers until his eyes went blurry.

His first plan was simple: start with the rice, because it was the biggest job. He measured out the cups and set the pot by the stove. Then he looked at the clock, which read 5:40, and did the math on the back of the recipe. If the rice started now, it would finish at six, and sit there getting cold and gluey for a whole hour. He frowned, erased his notes, and tried again. "Nothing to eat at seven," he muttered. "Cold rice and no curry. Great."

Then he flipped the paper over and wrote 7:00 at the bottom, and worked upward like climbing down a ladder. Flatbread last, since it was fastest, then rice, then curry first because it took longest. He made a schedule: curry on at 6:10, rice at 6:30, dough rolled by 6:45, flatbread on the pan at 6:50. He read it twice. It still felt backwards, starting with the longest thing instead of the easiest one, but the numbers lined up, so he decided to trust them.

The curry went into the pot right on time. The sauce turned turbulent as it boiled, bubbles rolling up and over one another, and he turned the heat down the way the recipe said. Then the neighbor, Mr. Swampy, knocked on the door to return a borrowed umbrella. He sniffed the air from the hallway. "Smells like somebody's got a plan," he said. Jake demonstrated the schedule by holding it up, pointing at the 7:00 at the bottom, and Mr. Swampy laughed. "Smart kid. My wife does the same thing every Sunday." Then he left, and Jake got back to work.

The rice went on at 6:30 exactly. While it cooked, he rolled the flatbread dough into circles, and his first three came out shaped like continents. He rolled them thinner and they got rounder. When the doorbell rang at seven, the curry was thick, the rice was fluffy, and he slid the last flatbread off the pan with a hiss.

Chelsea walked in carrying a bag of mango chutney, because she'd been sure he would forget something. She looked at the full table and her shoulders dropped a little. "I wanted to be the one who saved dinner," she said. There was a hint of resentment in her voice, and Jake recognized it, because it was exactly how he felt when his older brother fixed things for him. "You can demonstrate the chutney," he said, handing her a spoon. "Nobody eats curry without it." Precious was already scooping rice onto a plate. "Seven o'clock," she said, "and everything's hot. How?" Jake tapped his pencil against his list, right where the 7:00 was. "I started there and worked backwards."

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: The United States Homestead Act of 1862 offered 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on it and farmed it for five years.
story:
The library closed at eight, and Theodore's report was due first period tomorrow. He slid a thin book called Letters Home: A Settler's Diary across the table and dropped into the chair beside Brooks, who was already copying facts onto index cards.

"Mr. Korhonen said we need a primary source," Theodore said. "A real person's own words. Not a textbook paragraph about pioneers." He had grabbed three books off the shelf, and this was the last one, the one with a faded cloth cover and a photograph glued inside: a man in a wide-brimmed hat standing on treeless flat land.

He opened to the first entry and read silently, then out loud. "April the ninth. We have filed our claim at the land office. One hundred and sixty acres, and it will be ours if we stay and work it five years." Theodore stopped. "Sixty acres? No, one hundred sixty. Why such a big number?" Brooks shrugged and kept writing.

Theodore flipped forward, hunting. "Here, October. The wheat failed and the creek went dry, but Father says we cannot leave, for if we remain the full five years the land becomes ours." He sat back. "It's like a rule. The government wanted people to move west, so it made them a deal." He grabbed a fresh card and wrote it out, then tested it against another entry. "This one, two years later. A neighbour gave up and moved on, and his claim went back to the government. So the deal only works if you stay the whole five years."

Mr. Korhonen passed their table with a cart of returns and slowed down. "Finding something?" he asked. Theodore held up the diary. "The Homestead Act," Theodore said. "That's what the back cover calls it." Mr. Korhonen nodded and wheeled on toward the front desk.

Theodore kept reading while the daylight outside began to evaporate and the study lamps glowed luminous against the tall windows. One entry stopped him cold. "Our neighbour Mr. Pyle, a soldier with a small pension, has also claimed his quarter of land. He says a wounded man may still farm if his sons are strong." Theodore copied the sentence, because it showed something the textbook never did: people came for different reasons, and land was a promise that pulled them across the prairie.

At seven forty, the loudspeaker announced fifteen minutes until closing. Brooks groaned over his half-finished cards, but Theodore had three index cards, a quotation, and a page number. On the walk to the checkout desk, he stacked the cards in order and squared the edges against the counter. "You know what I like?" he said. "This guy wrote about the wind for three straight days, and he never quit." He slid the diary across to Mr. Korhonen. "Can I take this home tonight?"

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Correlation does not prove causation: two things rising together, like ice cream sales and sunburns, may both be caused by something else, such as hot weather.
story:
Mr. Park had taped a headline to the whiteboard before class: "Students Who Eat Breakfast Every Morning Score Higher on Tests." Underneath it, in marker, he had written one word: "Proof?"

"Look at this," Colton whispered to Trace, sliding the polymer lab worksheet aside. Their slime experiment could wait. "My mom cut that exact story out of the paper and taped it to the fridge. She's been making me eat eggs all week."

Trace shrugged. "So? Eggs are fine."

Mael leaned in from the next lab station. "My cousin read it too. She says breakfast makes your brain bigger."

Colton stared at the headline. Something about it nagged at him, the way a word on the tip of your tongue does. He thought about last summer, when he and Trace had tried to petition the ice cream truck driver to come to their street more often. They had noticed that on the days they bought the most ice cream, they also got the worst sunburns, and for a whole week Colton had believed the ice cream was causing the burns. Then Trace's older sister had laughed and said, "Correlation does not prove causation." Two things rising together, she told them, like ice cream sales and sunburns, may both be caused by something else, such as hot weather.

Colton raised his hand. "Mr. Park, my mom read an anonymous survey in that article. But what if the breakfast kids have something else in common? Like, their parents make them go to bed early, so they're just less tired?"

Mr. Park smiled but said nothing, which Colton had learned meant "keep going." So Colton turned to Trace. "Think about it. The kids eating breakfast every morning probably have somebody home in the morning making it. Maybe that same somebody makes them do homework."

"So the eggs don't get the credit," Mael said slowly. "The whole house does."

"That doesn't mean breakfast is bad," Colton added. "It just means this one story about one group of kids isn't proof of anything."

At the end of class, Mr. Park collected the slime containers, still wobbly and blue. "Colton, hold back a second." When the room had emptied, he pulled a folded paper from his desk and set it in front of him. Another headline, another survey about food and grades. "You want to figure out what this one's missing?"

Colton picked it up and read the first line twice. "Same trick," he said. "I bet they all have something else in common." He grabbed a pencil.

activity: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
knowledge_domain: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
fact: An ammeter measures current and must be connected in series, in the same loop as the wire, so the current flows through the meter.
story:
Riley spread his science project across the picnic table at the edge of the skate park: a battery, a coil of thin copper wire, a voltmeter, and an ammeter borrowed from Mr. Berg's classroom. His assignment was due Monday, and the whole thing came down to one number. He had to find the resistance of the wire using Ohm's law, which meant measuring the voltage across it and the current through it, then dividing.

Kaitlyn rolled up on her board, kicked it into her hand, and leaned over the table. "What's all this?"

"Resistance lab," Riley said. "You watch the meters and write down the numbers while I hold the clips." Kellen arrived next, sneakers crunching over the gravel, and sat down on the far side with the notebook.

Riley clipped the voltmeter to the two ends of the wire, then clipped the ammeter onto the battery terminal the same way, beside it. He switched on the circuit. The voltmeter moved, showing 6 volts. The ammeter sat at zero. He tapped its face. Nothing. He unclipped it, clipped it back on the same terminal, and it still read zero. "The meter's broken," he said. "Mr. Berg gave me a dead one."

Kaitlyn picked up the ammeter and turned it over. "Maybe it only reads when it's part of the loop," she said. "Right now it's just standing next to the wire."

Riley frowned at the table. The current flowed out of the battery, through the wire, and back. The ammeter was clipped on from the side, touching the terminal, but not in the path. He pulled the clip off the battery terminal and connected the ammeter between the battery and the wire instead, so the current had to pass through the meter to reach the wire at all. The needle jumped to 0.4 amps.

"It works," Kellen said, writing fast before the number could change.

"So an ammeter goes in series," Riley said. "In the same loop as the wire, so the current flows through the meter itself."

They ran the calculation twice. Six divided by 0.4 gave 15 ohms, and when they swapped in a longer coil of wire, the current dropped, as if the extra length could restrict it, and the resistance came out higher. That was the pattern: more wire, more ohms.

By the time the sun thinned out and the park went nearly barren, Riley had his verdict written in the notebook. The resistance of the short wire was 15 ohms. He packed the meters into his backpack, zipped it, and kicked his board up under his arm.

"Same table tomorrow?" Kaitlyn asked.

"Same table," Riley said, and rolled off down the path.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Growth plates, areas of growing cartilage near the ends of children's bones, are weaker than the bone around them, which is why young athletes have limits on repetitive stress.
story:
Harper counted her flip turns out of the corner of her eye the way you count ceiling tiles at the dentist. Forty-one in one practice. Her right shoulder had started complaining around turn twenty, and by turn thirty it was outright arguing. She pulled herself out of the pool at Sunset Aquatic Center and sat dripping on the edge while her teammate Leandro floated past like a manatee with a mission.

"Your face looks like your math homework," he said.

"My shoulder hurts. Same side, same spot, every Tuesday and Thursday." Harper rotated her arm slowly, like she was stirring an invisible cauldron. "It never hurts on weekends. Only after Coach makes us do a hundred wall pushes and all those turns."

Anna-Eve climbed out beside her, wringing water from her braid. "Maybe the pool is haunted. Tuesday ghost."

"Eliminate the ghost," Harper said, holding up one finger. "It hurts on Thursdays too, and everyone knows ghosts take Thursdays off." She was only half joking. Something was causing the pattern, and she wanted to know what, because the championship meet was in three weeks and she was seeded first in the hundred backstroke.

That night she found a note taped to her bathroom mirror, in her little brother's handwriting, which looked like spiders had fought a war on the paper: "Dear Harper. You know how I pitch in Little League? Coach won't let me throw past my pitch limit even in the playoffs. He says kids' bones have growth plates near the ends, growing cartilage, and they're weaker than the bone around them. That's why they limit our throwing. So maybe STOP DOING A MILLION TURNS. Also you used all the orange shampoo. This is a controversy. Love, your favorite brother."

Harper laughed so hard she snorted, then stopped laughing, because the note actually made sense. Growing cartilage, weaker than the bone around it, near the ends of kids' bones. A hundred repetitive wall pushes plus forty-one turns, twice a week, was exactly the kind of stress her brother's coach tried to limit.

The next morning she knocked on the door of the apartment across the hall. Mr. Bondarenko had been a swimmer in his day and kept his old medals in a cookie jar, which Harper considered the greatest fact she knew. She showed him her brother's note. He read it twice, nodding.

"Your brother is smarter than his spelling," he said. "Warm-ups, fewer high-rep sets, and you tell your coach about the shoulder today. Being brave enough to say it is half the training."

At practice, Harper walked over to the coach, and Anna-Eve gave her a double thumbs-up from lane three. "If you get benched," Anna-Eve called, "the ghost can have your lane."

"The ghost is transparent," Harper called back. "She'll blend right in."

activity: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
knowledge_domain: to run an eight-hundred-metre race pacing the first lap so there is energy for the second
fact: Running directly behind another runner shelters you from the wind, so following someone on the first lap can save energy for the finish.
story:
The eight-hundred-metre race was going to be run around the outfield of the baseball diamond, four little flags marking the corners, and James had blown it twice already. Both times he sprinted the first lap like it was the only lap, and both times the second lap ate him alive. Today Mr. Becker had drawn two circles in the dirt with his heel. "First lap is not the race," he said. "It's the price you pay for the second one."

James's friends were no help. Leonidas kept saying "just run faster," which was like telling a sinking person to swim harder. Simeon, who was a veteran of exactly three races and considered himself a sage, said James needed to "clarify his strategy," though when James asked what that meant, Simeon said, "You know. Plan stuff." The wind that morning was blowing hard across the back straight of the diamond, past the sparse line of parents in folding chairs, and James noticed something during the warm-up jog. When he ran behind Simeon, the wind seemed to vanish. When he pulled alongside, it slapped his face again.

He tested it three times, to be sure. Behind, easy. Beside, hard. Behind again, easy. It was like Simeon was a moving wall, and the wind hit him first. That meant a plan: stay tucked in behind someone on the windy back straight during the first lap, save everything, then spend it all on the second lap where the wind came from the side and nobody could shelter anybody. "You're breathing on my neck," Simeon complained during one test lap. "That's the plan," James said. "My plan involves your back."

At the start, James found himself next to a tall kid from another school who shot off the line like a rocket. Every muscle in James screamed to chase him, but he let the tall kid go and tucked in behind a runner in a green shirt instead. Around first flag, past the dugout, down the back straight the wind roared, but green shirt took it, and James sat in his pocket feeling almost lazy. His legs stayed fresh, quiet, coiled. Behind the plate, Leonidas cupped his hands and yelled, "You're in last-ish!" James had to smile, because last-ish on lap one was exactly the plan.

Second lap, he went. Off the green shirt's shoulder, past two kids who were suddenly running like their shoes were full of sand, around the third flag, and into the wind with a whole tank of gas left. He caught the tall rocket kid at second base, of all places, and passed him between the mound and home plate. He finished second overall, five steps behind a kid who'd paced it even better, and he didn't care. Mr. Becker checked his watch twice. "Your second lap," he said, "was faster than your first."

James walked the cooldown with his hands on his head, grinning at the clouds. Simeon jogged up beside him. "So my advice worked," Simeon said. "Your advice was 'plan stuff.'" "And look at you. Stuff planned." James laughed, then pointed at the tall kid, who was still bent over near the backstop. "Hey," James called. "Next time, run behind somebody on the windy part. Trust me. Best seat in the race." The kid looked up, red-faced and gasping, and gave him a slow thumbs-up.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A claim that cannot be checked even in principle, such as a vague promise that something 'changes lives,' gives readers nothing to test.
story:
The flyer was taped to the back of the seat in front of Jessica before she even sat down. bold letters across the top said "THIS CHANGES LIVES," and below that, in smaller print, "Join 10,000 students who already signed."

"Ten thousand," Constance said, reading over her shoulder as the bus lurched out of the loop. "That's basically everyone in town."

"Not everyone," Jessica said. "Our whole grade is only 260." She ran her finger down the page. The flyer wanted students to sign a petition asking the school board to switch to some new brand of tablet, and it promised that the tablets "would change lives forever." There was no name at the bottom, no website, nothing but an address in the mall where you could go to sign up.

Sirine leaned across the aisle. "My dad says that building closed during the recession. The mall lost like half its stores and nobody moved back in."

"So the address is fake?" Constance said.

"Maybe." Jessica folded the flyer into quarters and slid it into her binder. Something about it bothered her the way a loose tooth did, and she kept turning it over all the way to fifth period. "Changes lives" could mean anything. If the tablets arrived and nothing in her life changed, whoever printed it could just say, "Well, it changed somebody's life." There was no way to catch it in a lie. That was the thing she couldn't shake. A claim like that gave you nothing to test.

At the last bell she found Sirine by the gym and told her the idea. "We ask the company one question they have to answer with a number. Like, how many tablets, and by what date. If they dodge it, we don't sign."

"They'll dodge it," Sirine said.

"Then we'll see it happen."

The next morning they got to the bus stop early, and Mr. Bondarenko, their driver, was still wiping the windshield with a rag. "Mr. Bondarenko," Jessica called, "does a number ten bus go past the mall?"

He squinted at her in the mirror. "Route ten? Used to. Not since the recession. That whole wing's been dark for years."

Constance's mouth fell open. Sirine just nodded, like she'd already known and had been waiting for the rest of them.

Jessica pulled the flyer back out and read it one more time, slowly, following the intricate loops of the address with her fingertip. "Ten thousand students," she said out loud, "from a building nobody can get to."

"So do we still sign?" Constance asked.

Jessica tore the flyer in half, then in half again, and dropped the pieces in her pocket for the trash can at school. The bus hissed to a stop in front of them and opened its doors.

"After you," she said.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: The law of supply says that when the price of a good rises, sellers usually offer more of it, because making and selling it becomes more profitable.
story:
The parking lot of the gas station felt like the equator that afternoon, the sun hammering down on the pavement while heat shimmered above the pumps. Jeremy had set up a folding table beside his dad's truck, with a cooler of frozen juice pops he'd made the night before from leftover fruit punch. He and Ryan had appointed Ryan's older sister Ava as treasurer, since she was the only one with a cash box and the patience to count coins. They priced the pops at a dollar each, and for the first hour nobody stopped at all.

Ryan leaned against the truck and sighed. "I told you this was a bad spot. Everyone just fills up and leaves."

"I'm not being pessimistic," Ryan said when Jeremy frowned at him. "I'm being realistic. It's a gas station, not a fair."

Then the ice cream truck at the corner broke down. Jeremy heard the driver cursing at it, saw the small crowd of kids who'd been waiting in its shade drift toward the pumps with their dollars still in their fists. Within twenty minutes, the cooler was nearly empty and Ava was counting a surprising stack of singles. "Eighteen dollars," she said. "And we have four pops left."

"Raise the price," Jeremy said. It just came out of him, the way an idea does before you have checked it. "There's only four left and everybody still wants one. Charge two dollars."

Ryan thought that was greedy, but the last four pops sold at two dollars each in ten minutes, and two kids came up asking for more after they were gone. Ava wrote it all in a notebook, because she was like that. Jeremy stared at the empty cooler and felt something click. It wasn't that people had gotten hungrier. It was that the pops had gotten scarce, and the price had gone up, and they had still sold.

The next Saturday they came back with three coolers and a hand-lettered sign. They had barely set up when Jeremy noticed a girl from his street unfolding her own table across the lot, with a cooler of popsicles she'd clearly bought from the store freezer. Then two more kids arrived with homemade frozen lemonade in paper cups. By noon there were five stands.

Nobody sold much. At a dollar each, customers could take their pick, and Jeremy's table had a line exactly twice, both times for the mango ones nobody else had. On the drive home, Ryan counted the money, which came to eleven dollars each after they paid back Ava's dad for the punch. "So the high price was good for one week," Jeremy said slowly, watching the pumps shrink in the side mirror, "because nobody else was selling. But the high price was also like a signal. It told everyone selling pops was worth doing."

Ava snapped her notebook shut. "Next week," she said, "we sell mango."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Scooping flour straight from the bag packs it down, so a cup can hold much more flour than a recipe expects; weighing flour is more accurate.
story:
The community kitchen smelled like burnt sugar and dish soap. Georgia set her third failed batch of cookies on the counter and pushed the plate toward Yann, who poked one with a fork. It stood firm, like a hockey puck.

"They're dry again," Yann said. "And cakey. My grandma's are never like this."

Georgia pulled her recipe card out of her apron pocket. She had followed it twice, the same flour, the same butter, the same two eggs. "Same recipe, same oven, different cookies," she said. "So something has to be different that I can't see."

Mr. Virtanen, who ran the Saturday cooking class, was weighing bread dough at the next station. Georgia watched him set a metal bowl on his scale and zero it out. She began to hypothesize. Maybe the problem wasn't what she put in, but how much of it. Maybe her cups were holding more than the recipe expected.

She fetched the flour bag and a one-cup measure. First she scooped the cup straight down into the bag, the way she always did, leveled it, and dumped it onto the scale. Then she did it a second time, packing it harder, and a third time, gently. The numbers on the scale were all different. A cup could hold much more flour than the recipe meant, depending on how it went into the cup.

"Mr. Virtanen," she called, "does your recipe card for cookies have grams on it?"

He came over, wiped his hands, and looked. "Right there at the bottom. One hundred and twenty grams."

Her scooped cup had weighed a hundred and sixty. Georgia's pivot was immediate: she pushed the measuring cup aside and weighed out exactly one hundred and twenty grams of flour into a fresh bowl. Yann cracked the eggs while she creamed the butter and sugar, and this time the dough felt soft under the spoon instead of stiff.

While the new batch baked, Edouard arrived late from soccer practice and ate two of the hockey-puck cookies anyway. "Not bad," he said, "if you dip them in milk for a while."

"Flour is influential," Georgia told him, tapping the scale. "More than I thought. I'm weighing everything from now on." She slid the last dry batch off the counter and into the trash, then took a plate from the cupboard for the cookies that were already beginning to smell right.

The timer rang. Yann opened the oven door, and the cookies spread golden at the edges, slightly cracked on top. Georgia lifted one, broke it in half, and handed the warm piece across the counter. "Tell me that isn't better."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: After flying across time zones, the body clock adjusts at an average of about one day for each hour of time difference.
story:
Eleanor lay on the top bunk in the cabin at Rocky Pine National Park, staring at the ceiling. It was midnight, and her eyes felt like flashlights. Her little brother was snoring in the bunk below, and her parents were out cold too. The whole family had flown six time zones west two days ago, and somehow everyone else could sleep except her.

She crept down to the main room and found Hassan sitting at the table, eating crackers by the light of his phone. His family had driven in from the city to join the trip, and their cabin was right next door.

"Still awake?" he whispered. "Me too. My mom says we're broken."

"We're not broken," Eleanor said, but she frowned. On the first night, everyone had been awake until at least two in the morning. Tonight it was midnight and she felt wide awake, same as yesterday, just an hour earlier. She grabbed the park brochure and a pencil and started writing numbers on the back. Six hours of difference. Six nights of waking up too early, each one a bit better than the last.

"What are you doing?"

"Testing something," she said. "If we flew across six hours, and we're waking up about one hour earlier each night, then the pattern says the body clock fixes about one hour per day. So by day six, we should be normal." She tapped the pencil. "Tonight's night two. If I wake up at eleven tomorrow night instead of midnight, that demonstrates it."

Hassan grinned. "That's a long experiment. Want company? I'll bring snacks."

The next morning they hiked out to the overlook with Eleanor's brother and Mylee, Hassan's little sister, who complained that the trail was barren and boring. "No flowers, no animals, nothing," she said, kicking a rock. Eleanor spotted a lizard on a sun-warmed stone and pointed it out, and Mylee spent the next ten minutes photographing it from three angles. Later, when Mylee's water bottle ran dry, Eleanor shared hers without being asked.

That night Eleanor wrote a note and slid it under Hassan's cabin door. "Day three. Fell asleep at 12:30, woke at 11:15. Pattern holds. One hour per day, I think. Probability of me sleeping like a normal human by day six: very high. Bring pretzels." In the morning she found a reply on her own doorstep: "If your body clock is that stubborn, we can be nocturnal together. Hassan. PS Mylee says the lizard's name is Kevin."

By day six, Eleanor fell asleep at nine and woke with the sunrise, feeling like herself. She marched to the next cabin and knocked. Hassan opened the door, hair sticking up.

"Experiment complete," she announced. "Six hours, six days. I was right."

He rubbed his eyes. "Congratulations. Now can you demonstrate how to be quiet until eight?"

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: In March 1933, Joseph Goebbels became head of Nazi Germany's new Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda.
story:
The bus home from the museum smelled like rain and vinyl seats, and Riley held her notebook open on her knees even though the bus jolted so much her handwriting came out crooked. Her problem was simple and urgent: Monday's presentation on persuasion in advertising, worth a big chunk of her grade, and she had exactly one page of notes, most of them about a cereal box. Hanna slid into the seat beside her and leaned over to look.

"That's it? That's your whole presentation?" Hanna asked. Riley snapped the notebook shut.

"We spent forty minutes at those World War Two posters and I didn't write anything down. I was too busy staring." She opened the notebook again and stared at the empty page instead. "But there was something there. Something I missed."

Two seats ahead, Isobel was playing an audio clip from the exhibit on her phone, and Riley could hear the museum narrator through the tinny speaker. She leaned forward. "Isobel, play the propaganda part again."

Isobel held the phone between the seats. Riley listened with her pen ready. The narrator talked about the German government's posters from the 1930s: one poster showed a crowd of thousands of marching workers, as if everyone were already on the same side. Another used words like "parasites" and "traitors," words Riley realized weren't describing anything, they were weapons. A third showed a famous film director smiling, endorsing the regime. Riley wrote fast: crowd appeal, loaded words, celebrity endorsement.

"Wait," she said out loud. "This is the same stuff as the sneaker ads we looked up last week. Everybody's wearing them. Words like 'revolutionary.' The basketball star holding the shoe." She underlined her three notes three times. "The techniques aren't new. Somebody built them on purpose."

"Who builds a poster on purpose to lie to a whole country?" Hanna asked.

Riley flipped back through the exhibit pamphlet in her backpack, the folded paper Mr. Chowdhury had handed out on the museum steps. She smoothed it on her knees and found the panel about the posters, printed beside a small black-and-white photograph of a man at a desk. She read it twice to be sure.

"In March 1933, Joseph Goebbels became head of Nazi Germany's new Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda," she read aloud. "That was the ministry. That's who made the posters. It was a whole government department for it."

"So it wasn't just artists deciding to draw crowds," Hanna said slowly. "It was organized."

"It was a ministry," Riley said. "Like they had a department for it the way we have a department for roads." The bus lurched around a corner and her pen rolled; she caught it against the window. She thought of the contemporary ads she'd screenshotted on her phone, the ones from this year, and understood suddenly that the pattern ran underneath both, old poster and new commercial, like pipes under a street. Same machinery, different product.

Mr. Chowdhury stood up near the front as the bus slowed for their stop, holding the door rail. "Monday presentations, everyone. Riley, you're first, I believe."

She looked down at her page of crooked notes, which had stopped being one page and was becoming three. "Actually, Mr. Chowdhury, I think I've got something better than the cereal box."

"Show me," he said, and she held up the pamphlet as she stepped off the bus into the rain, already talking.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Pressing a string at its exact midpoint halves the length that vibrates, and the note rises by one octave.
story:
Alex had been dreading Saturday all week, because his guitar lesson had been moved from the music shop to Ms. Siddiqui's garage, and he still couldn't play the song the recital required. "This piece is mandatory for every student," she had told the class, tapping the sheet music. "Even the tricky part at the end."

The tricky part was the problem. The song asked him to play a high E, and every time Alex reached for it, the note came out dull or wrong. He sat on a folding chair between the lawnmower and a shelf of paint cans, picking at the string and wincing.

Jaxton, who lived next door and had wandered in through the side door, flopped onto an old cooler. "You've played that same string forty times."

"Because it's wrong." Alex plucked the open low E string, then slid his finger up the neck, hunting. The note climbed a little at a time, then a lot, then somewhere near the middle of the neck it jumped out at him, bright and clear. He froze. It was E again, the same note, only higher.

"That's the one," Jaxton said, sitting up. "That's the sound you kept missing."

Alex set the guitar flat across his knees and bent close to it, eyes narrowed like he was looking through a magnifying lens at the frets. He counted them from the nut downward, one by one, and his finger landed on the twelfth. Exactly halfway down the string. He pressed there and plucked, then lifted his finger and plucked the open string again. Same note, then same note, higher.

"So pressing it right at the middle," he said slowly, "makes the string act like half a string." He tested it again, and again, watching his own fingers like they belonged to someone else.

Ms. Siddiqui came in carrying two glasses of lemonade and handed one to each of them, since the garage was stuffy and Jaxton had already drunk from the garden hose twice. She watched Alex press the twelfth fret and play the open string, one after the other.

"You found it," she said.

"The twelfth fret," Alex said. "It's halfway. The string's only half as long there, and the note goes up a whole octave."

She smiled and let him keep going. Alex played the open string, then the twelfth fret, back and forth, until his fingers knew the distance without his eyes. Then he ran the passage from the recital song, and the high E rang out clean over the sound of Jaxton drumming happily on the cooler.

"One more time," Alex said, and moved his hand back to the twelfth fret.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: In the United States, the national Poison Help line is 1-800-222-1222, and it connects callers to a local poison control center at any hour.
story:
Nolan had agreed to babysit two-year-old Poppy because Ms. Leung had promised it would be easy, and because he wanted the twenty dollars for the skateboard wheel he'd been saving toward since March. Now he stood at the edge of the park's shady playground, Poppy on his hip, and stared at the small blue bottle in her fist. She had dug it out of the bottom of Ms. Leung's tote bag while he was pushing her on the swing, and somehow she had twisted the cap open. The label said all-purpose cleaner. A thin line of liquid ran down her chin, and she was smacking her lips like she'd tasted something interesting.

"Spit it out, Poppy," he said, prying the bottle away. She gave him a defiant look and clamped her mouth shut, which scared him more than crying would have.

He crouched under the pavilion roof and made himself think instead of panic. The question he couldn't see the answer to was how much she'd actually swallowed. A taste? A mouthful? He remembered his friend Vihaan saying once that toddlers put everything in their mouths but usually spit out anything bitter, because bitter meant poison to a brain still learning the world. That was a pattern, not a guarantee, but it gave him a testable idea: if the cleaner was truly nasty, there would be proof on her tongue. He sniffed the open bottle, then leaned close to Poppy's face and breathed in. Her breath smelled sharp and lemony, but there was no puddle on the ground and no dripping shirt. Probably a taste, then. Probably. The word "probably" was not good enough when a two-year-old was involved.

He pulled out his phone and called Ms. Leung, but it went to voicemail; she was at her meeting, which was the whole reason he was here. That was when he remembered the refrigerator. Back at her house, taped beside a magnet shaped like a lemon, there was a worn slip of paper he'd noticed while hunting for Poppy's juice cups. In big marker letters it said Poison Help: 1-800-222-1222. He had wondered at the time why anyone would tape a phone number to a fridge, and now he understood the whole phenomenon in one cold second.

He dialed Poppy's stroller in front of him and punched in the numbers while he walked, bouncing her when she fussed. A person answered before he finished his first sentence, which startled him; the sky was already going purple, well past five o'clock, and yet the line was live.

"This is the poison helpline," the woman said. "You've reached your local poison control center. It's staffed any hour, day or night. Tell me what happened." He did: the cleaner, the open cap, the smell on her breath, his guess that she'd only tasted it. The woman asked him to describe the label and Poppy's behavior, then told him what to watch for over the next hour and said to call back if anything changed.

"Can I really call at any hour?" he asked.

"Any hour," she said. "That's what we're here for."

He sat down on a bench with Poppy on his lap and read her the billboard ad across the street as if it were a picture book, just to keep his voice steady. She grabbed his thumb and tried to interpret his pointing as a game, shrieking with delight each time he tapped the giant hamburger. When Ms. Leung came jogging up the path an hour later, still in her meeting clothes, Nolan was still holding the empty bottle, and Poppy was asleep against his chest, breathing slow and lemony and fine.

activity: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
knowledge_domain: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
fact: The Treaty of Versailles, which ended the First World War between Germany and the Allies, was signed on 28 June 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles.
story:
The poster paper was blank and due on Friday, and Natalie still could not answer Mr. Zhou's question: how did the Treaty of Versailles help lead to the Second World War? She knew the treaty ended the First World War between Germany and the Allies, and she knew it made Germans furious. But "it made people mad" was not going to fill a whole poster.

"You need the date," said Bella at lunch, tapping the library book between them. "Mr. Zhou loves dates."

"I can memorize a date," Natalie said. "That's not the hard part." The hard part was the invisible part, the chain that connected a table in 1919 to tanks twenty years later. You could not see a cause. You had to build it.

The book had a photograph. Men in dark suits crowded along a long table, and behind them the wall was nothing but mirrors, window after window of glass. "What room is that?" Natalie asked. She ran her finger under the caption. The Hall of Mirrors, it said, at the Palace of Versailles. She read the sentence twice. The Treaty of Versailles, which ended the First World War between Germany and the Allies, was signed on 28 June 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles. Five years, almost to the day, after a bullet in Sarajevo had started the whole thing.

"France chose that room on purpose," Natalie said slowly. "Germany had declared itself an empire there before. It's like France was saying, remember this spot? Now we sign here." Bella looked at the photo again. "So the place is part of the message."

"That's my prototype," Natalie said, pulling out a marker. On scrap paper she drew a chain: treaty signed 28 June 1919, Germany loses land, money, pride, then anger, then a man who promises to fix all of it, then war. It was only a first version, rough and probably wrong in places, but it was something she could test.

Charles-Antoine leaned over from the next table. "You can't draw pride," he said. "It's not a thing."

"It doesn't have to be a thing you can touch," Natalie said. She drew an arrow instead. "It just has to point somewhere."

In class on Friday, Mr. Zhou walked the rows, stopping at desks, asking each of them to justify one link in their chain. When he reached Natalie's poster, he read the whole thing in silence. Then he pointed at her drawing of the mirrored room, small and careful in the corner. "Why did you put the room?"

"Because it's evidence," Natalie said. "The signing happened in the Hall of Mirrors at the Palace of Versailles on 28 June 1919, and France picked it. If they wanted a treaty that would last, they picked a strange way to say it. Humiliation doesn't fade like ink does."

Mr. Zhou looked at her for a moment, then wrote something in his notebook and moved on. Bella, two desks over, gave her a thumbs-up. After the bell, he handed the posters back face down, and Natalie flipped hers over to find a circle at the top of the page and, beside it, one underlined word: "Exactly."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: Box breathing means breathing in for a count of four, holding for four, breathing out for four and holding for four, then repeating the pattern.
story:
Grandpa's porch smelled like sawdust and coffee, and Jack had been staring at the same page of his history notes for ten minutes. Tomorrow he had to give a five-minute presentation in Ms. Silva's class, and every time he pictured himself standing up there, his stomach clenched and his hands went cold. His heart raced even though he was just sitting on a rocking chair doing nothing.

"You've been chewing that pencil like it owes you money," Grandpa said from the doorway.

Jack hadn't noticed he was doing it. That was the strange part. His body was acting stressed before his brain had even said anything. Last night he had tossed until midnight, and the night before that too. He started wondering if there was a hidden reason behind all of it, some pattern he was missing. Three bad nights of sleep, tight shoulders, a stomach that wouldn't settle. Maybe it was all one thing, not five separate problems.

"You nervous about something?" Grandpa asked.

"Presentations," Jack admitted. He was hesitant to say more, because saying it out loud made it real. "I always get like this. Quintin says he just doesn't care, and I don't get how."

Grandpa sat down across from him. "My mother used to say a worried body is like a bad diplomat, always announcing things before anyone agrees to announce them." He drew a square in the air with one finger. "This one came from the army. They call it box breathing. In for four, hold for four, out for four, hold for four, then start again."

Jack watched Grandpa's finger move: up the side of the invisible square while breathing in, across the top while holding, down while breathing out, along the bottom while holding again. Four sides, four counts each. Jack tried it. In, two, three, four. Hold. Out, two, three, four. Hold. His shoulders dropped maybe half an inch.

That night, Jack lay in the guest bed and decided to run an experiment on himself. Instead of lying there replaying every possible way tomorrow could go wrong, he would trace the square on the ceiling, over and over, and see if it changed anything. If it worked, that would tell him the sleepless nights weren't just happening to him. They were something he could act on. He counted and traced, counted and traced, and somewhere around the twelfth square he stopped noticing he was counting.

In the morning he felt almost normal. Before class, he sat at his desk and traced the square once more, one side for each count of four, while Payton flipped flashcards beside him. When Ms. Silva called his name, Jack stood up, took one slow breath, and looked at the poster that would depict the battle he was explaining.

"Okay," he said. "So, 1815."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: A 2001 study that observed children on school playgrounds found that other children were present during 88 percent of bullying episodes.
story:
The birthday party was in full swing in Mr. Sandhu's backyard, paper lanterns strung between the fence posts and half the grade seven class clustered around the snack table. Katherine was reaching for a second cupcake when she heard the laughter change pitch near the trampoline. Fraser was standing there holding his library book, and two boys she barely knew were doing impressions of the way he talked, drawing out every word like taffy.

Katherine's first instinct was to shout at them, but she remembered what had happened in October when she'd yelled at a kid in the hallway for shoving Joaquin. The kid had just gotten louder, and Joaquin had spent the rest of the week pretending he didn't know her. Something in that approach did not conserve anyone's dignity, least of all Fraser's, and she had been thinking about it ever since she'd done a class report on a real study. For the project she had read about a 2001 study that observed children on school playgrounds, and one finding had stuck in her head: other children were present during 88 percent of bullying episodes. Almost never was the target alone. There was almost always an audience, which meant there was almost always someone who could do something, if they could figure out what.

So Katherine tested a simple idea. Instead of confronting the two boys, she walked past them as if she hadn't noticed anything and stopped in front of Fraser. "There you are," she said, loud enough for everyone to hear. "You promised to settle the debate about whether that book counts as fantasy or a whole other genre. Joaquin's waiting. He says it's sci-fi, and he is completely wrong."

Fraser blinked at her, then caught on. "It's clearly fantasy," he said, clutching the book a little tighter. "There's a talking map."

"There is not a talking map."

"There is on page forty."

Joaquin, who was close enough to have heard the whole thing, drifted over and planted himself beside Fraser without a word. Joaquin never said much, but he was big, and he had a way of standing that made arguments seem like too much effort. The two boys looked around and discovered that their audience had wandered off to watch someone attempt a handstand on the trampoline. Laughter that nobody hears has nowhere to go, Katherine thought, and the impressions fizzled out like a sparkler in a puddle.

Later, while the candles were being lit, Fraser leaned over. "Thanks," he said quietly. "You didn't make it a thing."

"I saw a poster once," Katherine said, tearing her cupcake in half and handing him the bigger piece. "Some things work better anonymous." Fraser took the cupcake and grinned, and across the yard Joaquin gave them both a thumbs up as the lights went out and someone struck the first match.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Canada's first food bank opened in 1981 in Edmonton, Alberta.
story:
Elena stacked cans of beans on the shelf for the third time that morning and stepped back to look at it. At nine o'clock the shelf had been full. By ten it was half empty. Now, at almost noon, three rows gaped open again, and nobody had come through the door of the food bank in over an hour.

Makai slid a box of pasta along the floor with his sneaker. "Maybe the shelf is porous," he joked. "Like it drinks the cans."

"Shelves aren't porous," Elena said. "Sponges are porous. Rocks can be. Not metal." But she was already thinking. Food didn't vanish. Something took it, or moved it, and she hadn't seen what. She remembered her grandmother's old stone step, back when they lived in the grey house, the way green lichen crept across it so slowly you never caught it growing. You only noticed by comparing. She could compare too.

She counted the cans, wrote the number on a sticky note, and stuck it behind the rice bags where only she could see it. Then she told Ms. Wright she was going to sort boxes in the back room, and left a thin gap in the door instead of closing it.

Through the gap she watched the shelf. Dust drifted in the light from the window. Somewhere a radio played. She held still until her knees ached.

The door opened without the bell above it making a sound, which was strange, because the bell had rung for every other visitor that day. A woman Elena had never seen took four cans, quickly, quietly, and slid a folded paper under the tomato soup. Then she was gone.

Elena waited a full minute before she crossed the room and unfolded the paper. The handwriting was small and neat. "I fix the bell so it stays quiet when I come. I take for my neighbour who is too sick to leave his apartment. I leave this so you know. Thank you. I came here before, in 1981, when this food bank first opened in Edmonton, and I have never once been turned away."

Makai leaned over her shoulder, reading. "Whoa. 1981? That's before my parents were even born."

"It was the first one in Canada," Elena said slowly, because she'd read that on the poster in the hallway just an hour ago and hadn't believed a food bank could be that old. "The first food bank in the whole country, right here." All morning she'd been asking Angie how long the place had existed, and the answer had been hanging on the wall the entire time.

Ms. Wright came around the corner, saw the note, and smiled at nothing in particular. Elena checked her sticky note. Six cans gone, and now she knew exactly where.

She carried the note to the shelf, found the woman's earlier messages tucked behind the soup, a whole stack of them, and set the newest one on top. "We should keep these," she said. "And fix the shelf so there's always enough." She turned the paper over and wrote back, "Come anytime. The bell works better now."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: The Japanese word origami comes from 'ori', meaning to fold, and 'kami', meaning paper.
story:
The craft cabin at Camp Windrock smelled like glue and pine sap, and Jayden had eleven crumpled paper cranes piled beside his elbow like a small avalanche. He was supposed to fold one good crane by Friday for the camp art show, and so far every attempt collapsed at the same step, when the wings pulled free of the body.

"Mine keeps tearing too," Rebecca said, dropping onto the bench across from him. She held up a crane with a ripped tail. "Maybe the paper's bad."

Jayden smoothed one of his failures flat and studied it. It wasn't torn like hers. His simply fell apart, as if some fold underneath was loose. He couldn't see inside the finished shape, so he decided to test it. He folded a new crane slowly, and at the tricky step he pressed the hidden fold twice as hard with his thumbnail before shaping the wings.

Emilien wandered over from the pottery table and squinted at Jayden's project. "What's that called again? Oregami?"

"Origami," Rebecca said. "It's Japanese. Ori means to fold, and kami means paper."

"So folding paper," Emilien said. "Not cutting it or gluing it." He looked at his own hands, which were covered in dried clay. "I've been telling everyone at my table it means something about cranes."

"It just means folding paper," Rebecca said. "That's why we can't use tape, remember?"

Jayden barely heard them. His new crane held together, wings firm, and now he had an approximate answer to his problem: the hidden fold was the weak point, not the paper. He folded three more to be sure, and each one stood.

At lunch he showed Mr. Yamamoto, who ran the nature hikes and had stopped by the picnic tables. "Good spine," Mr. Yamamoto said, tilting the crane toward the sun. "The inside fold insulates the structure, like the hollow feathers on a duck."

Jayden grinned. He decided to keep testing. He tried thinner paper and it flopped. He tried an old postcard and it cracked at the fold. Heavier paper was the answer, but the camp supply bin had almost none, so he started a negotiation with the girl who ran the printmaking station, trading two of his finished cranes for three sheets of her heavy blue stock.

By Thursday afternoon he had a row of nine cranes on the windowsill, the blue one in the middle, wings open. Rebecca lined up her repaired crane beside them, and even Emilien, hands finally washed, left his clay and came to look.

"That one," Emilien said, pointing at the blue crane. "That's the one for the show."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Oil paint does not dry by water evaporating; its oil slowly reacts with oxygen in the air, so an oil painting can take days or longer to dry to the touch.
story:
Lily squeezed out a bead of cadmium red and dragged her brush across the canvas board, watching the sunset over the lake take shape. Tomorrow morning her painting had to be at the school art show, set up in the gym before the first bell. She had until bedtime to finish, and she had chosen oil paints because the colors blended like nothing else, exceptional, glowing, slow as honey. She worked until the moon on the water was finished, then touched the corner of the sky with one fingertip. The paint smeared. She frowned and wondered: how long could it possibly need? Her watercolors dried in minutes. "I'll just let it dry overnight," she told the cat, who blinked at her from the doorway.

When her friend Yasmin arrived after dinner to see the painting, Yasmin leaned close and then recoiled. "It's still wet? The show is in fourteen hours." Lily set the canvas in front of a small fan, angling the breeze across the sky. "Air will dry it," she said, sounding more certain than she felt. But was it moving air the paint needed, or something else in the air? She couldn't see what dried a painting. It bothered her, the way a hidden pattern always did, and she decided to test it.

She squeezed two tiny dabs of blue onto separate scraps of cardboard. One scrap she left on her desk, open to the room. The other she sealed inside a small glass vessel, a jar with a screw lid, so nothing could get in or out. If drying depended on moving air, the fan scrap should dry first and the jar scrap should dry too, just slower. If something in the air itself mattered, the sealed jar might not dry at all. She wrote both guesses in her sketchbook, then tried to think of a third possibility that could refute her whole plan, but she couldn't, so she went to bed with her alarm set for six.

At midnight she crept back down to check. The open scrap had gone tacky at the edges. The jar scrap was as glossy and wet as the moment she had squeezed it. She unscrewed the lid and held both scraps side by side, touching each with her pinky. Something in the air was being used up inside the jar, and outside, there was plenty of it. She lay awake turning the idea over. What did the air have plenty of? Oxygen. The oil was reacting with the oxygen, that had to be it, not water leaving like with her watercolors. That meant a whole painting could take days or longer to dry to the touch, and no fan in the world would hurry it much.

By morning the fan scrap had only skinned over, and her painting still held her fingerprint from the night before. She called Alistair, whose father painted portraits in their garage. Alistair put him on, and in the background a familiar voice said, "Tell her oil paint doesn't dry by water evaporating. The oil takes oxygen from the air. Mine took nine days once." Lily stared at the smudged lake. The show started in ninety minutes.

She could not carry a wet painting flat through a crowded gym. So she cut four corks in half, propped the painting face-up on a cookie sheet resting on the cork feet, and carried it like a tray of soup, slow and level, with Yasmin walking ahead clearing the way. At the sign-in table, the parent volunteer reached to take it, and Lily stepped back. "Careful," she said. "It's still drying. It might take days." The parent hovered her hand above the moon, felt nothing, believed nothing, and Lily kept walking, straight toward the easel marked with her name.

activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
knowledge_domain: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
fact: According to the CDC, nearly 9 out of 10 adults who smoke cigarettes daily first tried smoking by age 18.
story:
Olivia stood in the kitchen with her poster board spread across the counter and a marker uncapped in her hand. On Monday she had to explain, in front of the whole health class, how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway, and so far her poster said only the word NICOTINE in giant blue letters.

"Maybe Ms. Gill could tutor you," her mom said, sliding a glass of milk toward her. "She used to be a nurse."

"I don't need a tutor," Olivia said. "I need to understand it first." She had read the chapter twice. There were words like dopamine and receptors, and she could copy them, but copying was not explaining. If she stood up there and just recited vocabulary, Declan would whisper something and the whole class would laugh, and she would be humiliated in front of everyone, again, like the geography presentation in September.

She went upstairs and flopped on her bed, staring at the ceiling. Then she sat up. Her phone buzzed, and she picked it up even though she had meant to do homework. It buzzed again a minute later, and again, and she checked it every single time. She looked at the phone in her hand and felt something click. "The reward pathway," she said out loud. The brain got a little hit of good feeling, and it wanted to repeat whatever had caused it. That was the loop. She could not see her own brain, but she could see her own thumb.

She grabbed a shoebox, construction paper, and a marble. She cut a hole in one end and taped a paper ramp inside so the marble always rolled the same path, the way a signal always traveled the same route through the brain. When the marble dropped through the hole, a bell she had taped to the box rang. "Nicotine goes in," she said, dropping the marble, "the reward pathway fires, dopamine floods in, the brain says that was good, do it again." She dropped the marble five more times to test it. Every single time, the bell rang. The route was reliable. That was the whole trick of it.

Then Lilyanna called. "Did you see the graph in the chapter?" she asked. "The one about adults who smoke? It says according to the CDC, nearly 9 out of 10 adults who smoke cigarettes daily first tried smoking by age 18." Olivia wrote it down on the back of her hand. Nine out of ten. Almost all of them had started as teenagers, which meant their brains had gotten wired for it before they were even grown up. "That's why the tobacco companies care so much about teenagers," Lilyanna said. "If they don't hook us now, they basically miss their chance." Olivia stared at the number on her hand. Her brain was still under construction, which made the shoebox and the bell matter more than she had realized.

On Monday, Olivia carried the shoebox to the front of the room. Declan smirked, but she dropped the marble and the bell rang out clear across the silent classroom. "That's your brain on nicotine," she said. "Every time, the same pathway, the same reward, and the brain asking for more." Then she held up her hand with the fact written on it. "And according to the CDC, nearly 9 out of 10 adults who smoke cigarettes daily first tried smoking by age 18. That's not a coincidence. That's this bell."

Ms. Gill was sitting in the back, observing for the principal, and Olivia saw her nod slowly. When Olivia sat down, Lilyanna leaned over and whispered, "That box was radical." Olivia grinned and dropped the marble one more time under her desk, just to hear it ring.

activity: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
knowledge_domain: to compare the climate of a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature graphs
fact: A rainforest climate graph shows a nearly flat temperature line, because temperatures there stay warm and change little from month to month.
story:
Louis had two climate graphs taped to the kitchen table and a problem shaped like a stick. The assignment said to compare a desert and a rainforest using rainfall and temperature, and Jason had already texted him a drawing of a camel wearing sunglasses, which was not going to earn either of them a grade. The desert graph was easy. Its temperature line swooped up and down like a roller coaster, and the rainfall bars were so short Louis had to squint to see them at all. The rainforest graph, though, looked broken.

The temperature line on the rainforest graph ran almost perfectly flat. Month after month, it just lay there. Louis checked the printer, then the website he'd printed from, then his own eyes. He texted Jason: "my rainforest graph is busted." Jason texted back a shrugging emoji, which was helpful to no one.

Louis leaned closer. The rainfall bars were fat all year round, so it wasn't as if the graph had no information. It was just that the temperature refused to do anything. He tried an experiment. He covered the month labels with his thumb and tried to guess which month he was looking at. On the desert graph he could guess, sort of, by whether the line was climbing or falling. On the rainforest graph he guessed twelve times and got it right once, which was about what you'd get from a coin with a lot of sides. He moved his thumb. "December," he read, and then, further along, "June." Same spot. Same flat line.

So the graph wasn't broken. That was the illusion. It looked empty because nothing changed, and nothing changing was the whole point. He wrote it in his notebook: rainforest temperatures stay warm and barely shift from month to month, so the line sits flat, unlike the desert's, which leaps around. It felt strange to write "nothing happened" as an answer, and he checked it three times to make sure it didn't contradict the graph. It didn't. The graph agreed with itself, smugly.

When his mom called that dinner was ready, Louis peeled the tape off the table and carried both graphs to his room. He took a photo of the flat line and sent it to Jason with the caption "guess the month." Jason texted back "March? August? I give up." Louis typed his reply, grinning at the ceiling: "All of them. Every single one. Deserts are exceptional drama queens, but rainforests don't even blink." Then he pinned the rainforest graph above his desk, flat line and all, and went down for dinner.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Chinese culture, a clock is usually avoided as a gift, because the phrase 'giving a clock' sounds like a phrase about attending someone's death.
story:
Max pressed his nose against the glass of the thrift shop window on Friday afternoon, staring at the brass clock inside. It was small and round, with a face like a sun, and it cost six dollars. His mother had said he could spend up to ten on a housewarming gift for the Lins, who had just moved in next door with their granddaughter Mei, and Max wanted the clock the moment he saw it. New house, new clocks, that seemed logical to him.

"It's perfect," he said to Harman, who had tagged along with his backpack still on one shoulder.

"It's a clock," Harman said. "It tells time. That's it. That's the whole gift."

"A nice clock," Max said. "For a wall. In a kitchen." Mei was in his grade, and she had shown him the Lins' empty kitchen wall on Tuesday, the spot where nothing hung yet.

At school on Monday, Max was still carrying the idea around like a coin in his pocket. He set the clock on the desk during study hall, planning to wrap it in art class, when Angelica leaned over from the next row and frowned at it.

"Is that for the Lins?" she whispered. "You're giving them a clock? For their housewarming?"

Max noticed that she did not say "nice clock" or "good choice." She said "a clock," the way Harman had, as if the word itself were the problem. He started turning it over in his mind. Mei's grandmother had smiled at everything Max had ever said, so he could not ask her. But Mei was at the far table, and Mei would tell him the truth, because Mei always told the truth, even the time she said his shoe still had gum on it two days after he had scraped it.

He walked over, holding the clock behind his back like a game show prize. "Mei, if somebody gave your family a clock, for the new house, would that be okay?"

Mei looked up from her vocab sheet. "In Chinese culture, a clock is usually avoided as a gift," she said. "Because the phrase 'giving a clock' sounds like a phrase about attending someone's death."

"Oh," Max said. The sun-faced clock felt heavy now. "Good thing I asked."

"You should get food," Mei said. "My grandma loves food. Everybody's grandma loves food. That's the consensus in my family."

In art class, the group reached its own consensus around the paint-splattered table. Angelica suggested a mug, Harman suggested a plant, and Ms. Yoon, passing by with a stack of papers, paused long enough to say, "A fruit bowl never goes wrong," before moving on. Max thought about the Lins' kitchen, the empty wall, the table with nothing in its center. A bowl could sit there. A bowl could hold oranges.

After school he walked back to the thrift shop. The cashier found a blue ceramic bowl with a crackled glaze like ice on a pond, and Max counted out his ten dollars. He carried it to the Lins' door in a paper bag with tissue paper bunched on top, and Mei's grandmother opened it and held the bowl up to the light.

"It's beautiful," she said, then disappeared into the kitchen and came back with six oranges in it.

"See?" Mei whispered from the hallway. "Told you."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Baking powder already contains both baking soda and a dry acid, so it can make batter rise without an acidic ingredient in the recipe.
story:
Kayla counted the coins in her pocket as she walked between the stalls. The farmers' market came before the baking, and the baking came before everything else, because her parents were both working late and dinner was her job tonight. She needed eggs, butter, and buttermilk for the pancake recipe her grandmother had written on a card years ago.

At the egg stall she ran into Kyler and Brooklynn, who were sharing a bag of kettle corn. "Pancakes for the whole family," Kayla told them. "Six of them, including my grandmother, and she judges everything." Brooklynn laughed, and the laugh was infectious, so that even Kyler, who had sworn he hated the market, was grinning by the time they reached the dairy stand.

The trouble started at home. Kayla lined up her ingredients on the counter in the order the recipe demanded, because in her mind a recipe had a hierarchy: the rising agent came first, then the wet ingredients, then everything else. She reached for the tin marked baking powder and found only a few dusty grains at the bottom. The box of baking soda, though, was nearly full. Soda, powder, close enough, she thought, and stirred a spoonful into the batter along with regular milk instead of buttermilk, since she'd spent her last dollars on eggs and butter.

The first pancake came out flat and dense, pale, with a faint bitter edge. Kayla set it on a plate and stared at it. The second one, same batter, came out the same. She flipped the recipe card over and found a note in her grandmother's handwriting: "If you only have baking soda, use buttermilk or lemon juice in the milk." Kayla read it twice. So the soda needed something, and the powder was different somehow. She looked at the flat pancakes, then at the recipe's original instruction, plain baking powder with ordinary milk, and a thought formed. The powder must already have in it both the soda and something acidic, something dry, because the old recipe asked for no acidic ingredient at all and it still rose.

She had no lemon juice, but she did have the tail end of a carton of buttermilk she'd forgotten in the back of the fridge. She mixed a fresh batch, this time with the baking soda and the buttermilk together, and poured a circle onto the hot pan. Bubbles rose across the surface and the edges set. She flipped it, and the pancake came off the pan golden and thick.

At dinner her grandmother took the first bite, chewed, and nodded once. "These rose properly," she said. Kayla put the syrup bottle in front of her and said, "Wait till you hear how I found out why."

activity: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
knowledge_domain: to stand up for a classmate being teased without making the situation worse
fact: Saving screenshots of hurtful online messages gives a trusted adult a record to act on, since messages can be deleted later.
story:
The group chat lit up during lunch, and Brooklyn watched Mahdi's face change before he even said a word. His thumb hovered over the screen, and then his shoulders dropped. At the next table, Zayden and two other boys were grinning at their phones.

"What did they send?" Brooklyn asked, sliding onto the bench beside Mahdi.

He turned his phone toward her, but the screen was already blank where three gray bubbles had been. "They posted something about my backpack," he said. "Then they deleted it. Now it's just gone."

Last month something like this had happened to Brooklyn herself. She remembered standing in the gym with her phone shaking in her hand, trying to show Mr. Traoré what a girl had written about her shoes, and finding nothing but empty space. Mr. Traoré had wanted to help. He had said the words, but without the posts themselves it was her word against theirs, and everyone knew how that ended.

That was when a thought clicked into place, quiet and certain. The messages had disappeared, but they had existed first. Deleted did not mean never there. If a message could be seen, even for ten seconds, it could be captured. She tested the idea in her head: the next time something mean appeared, she would screenshot it before it vanished, and there would be a record no deletion could erase.

"Send me the chat invite," she told Mahdi. "I'm going to stay in it."

"You'll just get teased too," he said.

"Maybe." She picked up her milk carton and peeled it open. "But I'll be watching."

That afternoon, during silent reading, her phone buzzed against her hip. She glanced down under the desk. A new message from Zayden: a photo of Mahdi's backpack with a caption about kids who could not afford real ones. Her heart thumped so hard she could hear it in her ears, like a drum under wet paper. She took a screenshot. Then another, because her first shot had caught only half the caption. The message sat on the screen for maybe forty seconds before it winked out of the chat, and she thought about how quick Zayden was to erase his own words, as if speed could make them innocent.

At dismissal she found Mahdi by the water fountain, where the hallway smelled like floor wax and old oranges. "Come on," she said. "We're going to Mr. Traoré."

"I don't want to make it worse," Mahdi said. He pressed the fountain button and let the water run without drinking.

"It won't be worse. It'll be proof." She held up her phone. "They can delete the chat. They can't delete this."

In Mr. Traoré's classroom, the afternoon sun striped the desks in gold. He looked at the screenshots for a long time, and his jaw tightened. "Do you know what would have happened if you hadn't saved these?" he asked. "Nothing. I would have had nothing. It would have been negligent of me to punish anyone on guesswork, and Zayden knows most kids delete the evidence before an adult sees it."

"It's not guesswork now," Brooklyn said. "It's a record."

Mr. Traoré nodded slowly. "We'll integrate this into how the class handles online behavior from now on," he said. "But that's tomorrow's problem. Today, we deal with this."

Zayden was called in from the yard. He walked in with his chin up, like someone who believed the trail had been wiped clean. Then Mr. Traoré turned the phone around, and Brooklyn watched the confidence drain out of him the way water drains from a sink, all at once and then in slow spirals.

"They were jokes," Zayden said.

"That's not a verdict you get to hand down yourself," said Mr. Traoré. "Ask Mahdi what they felt like."

Mahdi looked at the floor, then up. "They felt like you wanted me to leave the school," he said quietly.

Zayden did not answer. Outside the window, a crow landed on the fence and tilted its head, watching them all through the glass.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: The 'fundamental attribution error', named by psychologist Lee Ross in 1977, is the habit of blaming someone's behavior on their character while overlooking the situation they were in.
story:
Jasmine had been rehearsing her speech all the way down Maple Street, and now Billy was right there at his mailbox, so she had to say it or choke on it. "You skipped my birthday sleepover. Everyone came. Even Luca came, and he lives across town."

Billy shoved a flyer into the mailbox slot without looking at her. "Yeah. I know."

"That's it? That's all you've got?" She remembered the night before, the sleeping bags spread across her living room floor, the empty spot near the window where Billy always claimed first. She had checked the door every time a car passed. "You didn't even text."

"My phone died. And I had to go somewhere." He turned toward his house, and she noticed his sneakers were untied and his backpack hung off one shoulder, bulging like he'd packed in a hurry.

"Go where?" she demanded.

He stopped on the porch steps. "The hospital. My grandma had a stroke Friday afternoon. My mom drove us straight there and I didn't get home until this morning." His voice cracked on the last word.
