Jasmine felt the ground shift under the whole argument she'd built in her head. She had decided Billy was selfish, that he'd chosen video games over her, that their friendship since second grade meant nothing to him. Every missing text had become more proof. And now all of it looked different.

"Wait," she said. "I thought you just bailed. I invented a whole version of you."

"That's rough," said Mr. Han, who was pruning his hedge next door. He clipped a stray branch and added, "My students do that too. We blame character and skip the situation. There's a name for it. Fundamental attribution error. Some psychologist, Lee Ross, called it that back in 1977."

Jasmine stared at him. "That's a real thing?"

"Look it up," Mr. Han said, turning back to his hedge.

"Can I come in?" she asked Billy. "Even for ten minutes?"

Billy's mom opened the door before he answered. She was carrying a lasagna pan toward the kitchen, and she gave Jasmine a tired smile. "Billy's hoping to visit Grandma again tonight if visiting hours allow it. He's been making her a card all morning. He wants it to be perfect."

"I'm using the laser printer for the lettering," Billy said. "It's supposed to say get resilient soon. Well, get well soon, but with a joke she'll get. She survived worse."

"Can I help?" Jasmine asked. "I'm decent with markers, and I can transform a plain card into something with actual glitter, if you want."

Billy hesitated, then pushed the door wider. "Bring the silver markers. Grandma hates glitter."

She ran home for them, and when she got back he was holding the door open.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Detergent molecules have one end that is attracted to water and another end that is attracted to oil and grease, so they lift greasy dirt off fabric into the wash water.
story:
The pizza stain on Norah's favorite yellow shirt looked like a small orange map of a country nobody wanted to visit. She had leaned over her slice at Emelia's birthday party, and the grease had thwarted her at the exact moment she thought she was being careful. Her mom was working late, so Norah had volunteered to do the laundry herself, which felt like a big-kid job until she stood in the Suds City Laundromat with a garbage bag of clothes and no idea where to start.

She spread everything across two plastic benches and began sorting. Darks in one pile, lights in another, and the yellow shirt alone in a third, like it was contagious. Her neighbor Mr. Leung was folding towels by the window, and when her quarters kept getting rejected by the machine, he walked over with a handful of coins and a grin. "This machine eats money when it's in a bad mood," he said. "Try sliding them in slower." She did, and the drum thumped to life.

Then came the shirt. Norah held it under the sink and rubbed the stain with plain water, hard, until her knuckles ached. Nothing. The orange map remained exactly where it had been, stubborn as ever. "It's not going to work," Emy-Jade said, appearing beside her with Emelia, both of them damp from the rain outside. "My mom says grease laughs at water. It just sits there." Norah frowned. Water cleaned mud off her sneakers. Why would grease be different? Mud was dirt stuck on top of fabric, but grease felt like it was part of the fabric now, soaked in and settled, and no amount of rinsing would lift something that was holding on from inside.

She turned the detergent box over and read the back, mostly to prove Emy-Jade wrong. The words surprised her. Detergent molecules, the box said, have one end that is attracted to water and another end that is attracted to oil and grease, so they lift greasy dirt off fabric into the wash water. She read it twice. "A molecule with two different ends," she said slowly. "One half wants water, one half wants the grease." Emelia leaned in to see. "So it's like a tiny rope," Norah went on, "with one hand grabbing the grease and the other grabbing the water, and when the water goes down the drain, it tows the grease along with it." Emy-Jade squinted at the box, then at the shirt. "Prove it."

So Norah made the stain's washing machine debut a solo event. She measured the detergent, dropped the shirt in, and set the warm cycle. While it agitated, the three of them ate the crackers Emelia had smuggled in her backpack, and Mr. Leung told them about the time a customer's dog fell asleep in a laundry basket and got accidentally folded. Nobody laughed harder than Norah, which made her laugh even more, the way spontaneous giggling always sneaks up on you.

When she pulled the shirt out, she held it up to the fluorescent light and turned it around twice. The orange map was gone, not faded but gone, and she said, "Told you. Rope."

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: At 5 percent interest compounded once a year, $1,000 grows to $1,276.28 after five years.
story:
William stood at the bank kiosk in the middle of the mall, holding his grandfather's letter in one hand and his dad's old calculator in the other. The letter said: "Put away your $1,000 birthday money for five years, and I'll add $250 at the end if you don't touch it." It sounded great until Wesley had leaned over his shoulder at school and said, "My cousin says banks do something better. Ask about compound interest."

Now Wesley and Farrah were with him at the mall, pretending to shop while William worked up the nerve to talk to the bank clerk behind the counter. Farrah nudged him. "Just go. You already did the math your grandfather's way, right?"

William nodded. He had done it on paper last night. Five percent simple interest on $1,000 was $50 a year, which made $250 after five years, plus the original thousand. Exactly what his grandfather was offering. If the bank could beat that, he'd take the bank. If not, he'd take the deal that came with a hug at Christmas.

The clerk, a young woman with a name tag, tapped her screen when William asked. "Five percent, compounded once a year," she said. "Compounded," William repeated, and Wesley whispered, "That's the word my cousin used." The clerk turned the screen toward him so he could read the number himself.

William's stomach tightened as he stared at it. $1,276.28. He checked it against his own paper, finger moving down the column, and there it was: the bank's total was $1,276.28 while his grandfather's offer came to $1,250. The difference was $26.28, more than enough for the video game he'd been saving nothing toward because he had nothing to save. He almost laughed out loud in the middle of the mall.

"You look like you just won something," Farrah said.

"Twenty-six dollars and twenty-eight cents," William said. "The bank wins."

His face went hot anyway, because across the food court he spotted his grandfather buying a coffee, wearing his ridiculous green camouflage jacket like he was on a secret mission instead of a mall errand. William folded the letter and hurried over before he could lose his nerve.

"Grandpa, your deal is really good," he said. "But the bank pays $1,276.28 after five years, and yours is $1,250. Can I still get the hug at Christmas?"

His grandfather laughed so hard he nearly spilled his coffee. "Take the bank, kid. And buy something nutritious with that extra money, not candy."

"I'm buying a game," William said.

activity: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
knowledge_domain: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
fact: Ohm's law says voltage equals current times resistance, so a wire's resistance is found by dividing the voltage across it by the current through it.
story:
The garage smelled like oil and cold metal, and Lucy had exactly one hour before her mom came to drive them home. Cataleya tapped the voltmeter against the coil of copper wire stretched between two clamps on the workbench, and Natasha held the phone like it might bite her.

"The judge packet says we have to report the resistance of our test wire tomorrow," Natasha said, reading the screen for the third time. "It says it right here. Resistance, in ohms. We don't have an ohm number anywhere."

"We have two numbers," Lucy said. "That's something." The voltmeter glowed 4.5, steady as a heartbeat. The ammeter, wired in line behind it, read 0.9. She stared at them both, waiting for a third number to appear out of nowhere, which it did not.

Cataleya groaned and slid down to sit on an old boat cushion. "This garage is freezing. Why couldn't your dad keep his fishing boat stuff somewhere with heat?" The boat trailer loomed over them, and beyond the open garage door the estuary lay gray and flat, its brackish water sliding in with the tide. Lucy's dad patched nets there most Saturdays. He kept the whole setup in this garage because it was the only room with a bench long enough for a test wire, and right now the bench was their whole science project.

Lucy closed her eyes and let herself drift back to Tuesday, to Ms. Cho standing at the whiteboard in the lab. Ms. Cho had written V, I, and R on the board and said, "Ohm's law. Voltage equals current times resistance. That's the whole thing." Then she had assigned the reading and walked off, refusing to say another word about it, which at the time had seemed unfair and now seemed like a dare. Voltage equals current times resistance. Lucy turned it over in her mind. V equals I times R. If that was true, then R had to be V divided by I. She grabbed a pencil.

"Cataleya. Four point five volts across the wire, and zero point nine amps through it. If voltage equals current times resistance, then resistance is voltage divided by current." She scratched the numbers across the back of a bait catalog. "Four point five divided by zero point nine."

Natasha leaned over her shoulder so hard she nearly knocked the pencil away. Cataleya stood up from the cushion, and for a moment all three of them watched the pencil move, the way you watch a bobber when a fish might be under it.

"Five," Lucy said. "Five ohms. That's our number."

"Check it," Cataleya whispered. "Multiply back. Zero point nine times five."

"Four point five volts," Lucy said. "Equivalent to what the meter says. It works both ways."

Natasha typed 5 into the form and hit submit at 8:59, one minute before the deadline. The confirmation chime sounded just as the wind off the estuary rattled the garage door, and somewhere out on the water a boat horn had not yet ceased its low moan.

"Six a.m. tomorrow," Cataleya said, pulling the clamps off the wire. "We're going to regionals."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: James Naismith invented basketball in December 1891 at a YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts, using peach baskets as the goals.
story:
Michael had the best seat in the living room, the corner of the couch where the cushion was worn soft, and he wasn't giving it up for anyone. The championship game was tied with two minutes left, and every commercial break felt like a held breath. Zayden sat on the floor with his back against the coffee table, and Ty kept pacing to the kitchen and back, though he refused to say why.

During a timeout, Zayden squinted at the screen. "Why do they even call it a basket? There's no basket anywhere. It's a hoop with a net."

Ty groaned from the doorway. "Who cares? We're watching the finals and you're asking about words."

"I care," Zayden said. "It's a real question."

Michael thought about it. He remembered a school report from last fall, and a small picture that had accompanied the page of text he'd read: an old gym with two peach baskets nailed up high. "It's because of how the game started," he said slowly, testing the memory against Zayden's question. "James Naismith invented basketball in December 1891. He was at a YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts, and he used peach baskets as the goals. Actual peach baskets. So the name stuck even after the baskets turned into hoops."

Zayden turned around fully. "Peach baskets? Like, fruit baskets?"

"That's what the picture showed."

Ty drifted back into the room, and Michael could tell the pacing had a purpose now. Ty's little sister had bet him a week of dish duty that the blue team would win, and Ty wanted the opposite result more than he wanted the snacks he kept pretending to fetch. He sat down at last, right on the armrest, eyes locked on the screen.

The flashback played in Michael's head while the players set up for the final possession: his desk in October, the librarian sliding the basketball book toward him, the tiny photograph of that old gym. He'd almost skipped that chapter. He was glad now that he hadn't, because Zayden was grinning up at him like Michael had pulled a coin from behind his ear.

The blue team's guard drove the lane, pulled up, and let the ball fly. It dropped through the net with a sound like a small tsunami sweeping the whole room off its feet, everyone shouting at once. Ty sank onto the carpet, head in his hands, already calculating the cumulative total of seven nights of dishes.

Zayden nudged Michael's sneaker. "So if they still used peach baskets, would that shot even have gone in?"

Michael smiled. "Somebody would've had to climb up and get it out."

On the screen, the crowd spilled onto the court, and the peach-basket story went with Michael, quiet and complete, all the way through the trophy ceremony.

activity: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
knowledge_domain: to compare how two faiths explain what happens after death
fact: Jewish views of the afterlife vary widely: Orthodox Judaism holds to a future resurrection of the dead, while Reform Judaism puts more weight on how people live now.
story:
The screen door banged behind Alexis as he carried the lemonade tray out to Grandpa's porch. Grandpa's knee was acting up again and the doctor had restricted him to short walks, so the whole afternoon would happen right there, between the rocking chair and the swing. Asha was already sprawled on the swing, and their cousin Nathanael sat on the top step, still in his nice clothes from synagogue. On the porch rail, a bowl of peppermints rattled whenever the wind touched it.

Asha had brought her question notebook, the one she filled with things for the ethics project. "I need two religions on what happens after you die," she said. "My pastor says heaven. What does Judaism say?" Alexis had assumed this would take thirty seconds. He even felt a little proud, the way you feel before you find out you were naive about something.

"Ask Grandpa," Alexis said. Grandpa set down his glass. "In our Reform synagogue, we mostly focus on how you live now. Being good, repairing the world, today." Asha wrote it down. Then Alexis turned to Nathanael. "Same question." Nathanael straightened his collar. "At our synagogue we hold that the dead will be resurrected. Resurrection, actually coming back to life, at the end of days." Alexis looked between them, one in the rocking chair, one on the step.

"You're both Jewish," Alexis said slowly, "but you gave opposite answers." He had a theory forming, and he decided to test it the way Asha tested things: same question, different source. "Nathanael, does everyone at your synagogue say resurrection?" "Yes, it's what Orthodox Judaism teaches," Nathanael said. "And Grandpa, everyone at yours?" "We put the weight on living now," Grandpa said, and popped a peppermint. "Jewish views vary widely, Alexis. We're one family and two answers, and there are more besides."

Asha's pencil stopped. "So I can't write 'Judaism says.'" "You can write that Jewish views vary widely, and give both," Alexis said. "That's actually a better project, because it's really two answers in one house." He liked the way the puzzle fit together, better than a single answer would have. Grandpa laughed quietly. "I learned that from a colleague at the hospital, years ago, an Orthodox chaplain. We argued about it every lunch break for a decade and remained friends."

The wind turned the pages of Asha's notebook and she flattened them with her palm. Then she wrote at the top of a clean page, "Same question, two synagogues," and underlined it twice. "Next summer," she said, "we ask the whole porch."

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: Open-ended questions, which cannot be answered with just yes or no, usually get longer answers and keep a conversation going.
story:
Stella got there five minutes early, which she decided was better than ten minutes early, because ten would look desperate and five just looked lucky. Whitney had walked over with her, mostly to give advice. "Ask him questions," Whitney had said at the door. "People love that."

Breanna scooped their cones behind the counter, waving with the scoop still in her hand. Stella ordered mint chocolate chip in a cup, because a cone on a first date was an accident waiting to happen, and then Marcus arrived. Not Marcus, actually. His name was Dominic, and he was in her science class, and he was now standing there holding a strawberry cone and looking at the floor tiles like they were fascinating.

"Do you like science class?" Stella asked.

"Yeah," he said. Then he ate some ice cream.

"Is mint chocolate chip good?" he asked back.

"Yeah," she said. Then she ate some ice cream. Stella wondered how two people could both be trying and still produce a silence this robust. It sat between them like a third customer at the table.

She thought about her little brother, who could talk for ten minutes straight about a beetle. Nobody asked him yes or no questions. They asked things like "What does it eat?" and he was off. Maybe the shape of the question was doing something. A yes or no question could be answered and then it was done, like a door that only opened once. But a question like "What's your favorite..." demanded more than one word.

"What's the best thing you've ever eaten?" she tried.

Dominic looked up from the tiles. "Okay, so, my grandma makes this soup, and it has this cheese in it that you can only get at this one store, and my cousin once ate six bowls and threw up, but he said it was worth it." He stopped. "That was too much information, wasn't it?"

"It was the perfect amount of information," Stella said, and she meant it.

They talked for forty minutes, about soup and about whether cats know their own names and about the time Dominic tried to contradict his gym teacher and got sent to the office. When the girl at the next table dropped her whole sundae on the floor and started to cry, Dominic immediately asked if she wanted half of his, and Stella thought, with a small jolt of something like compassion mixed with hope, that she might actually like this person.

Breanna leaned over the counter on her way past with a rag. "You two have been here for an hour," she said. "Another round?"

"One more scoop," Stella said. "Ask him about the cheese store."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Eid al-Fitr is the Muslim celebration marking the end of Ramadan, the month in which many Muslims fast from dawn until sunset.
story:
Owen's family arrived at the cultural center on Eid morning, and Demi trailed behind them holding a box of dates like it might go off. "I didn't eat breakfast," Demi whispered, "because I figured there wouldn't be any until later. Was that right?"

Owen considered this. He knew the shape of the month from watching his parents: the plate of dates set out before sunrise, the long hungry stretch through the school day, the moment the sun touched the rooftops and everyone could finally eat. But he hadn't thought about how it looked to someone seeing it from outside. "That's not how it works anymore today," he said, and then stopped, because he wasn't sure he could say why.

Inside, the hall smelled of cardamom and butter. Ms. Yoon, who taught art at the community classes, was arranging paper lanterns along the stage, indifferent to the chaos of children weaving under her ladder. Owen's aunt pressed food on everyone who passed. "You look thin," she told Demi, who was not thin, and piled a bowl with rice and lamb before Demi could answer.

Demi picked up a date, turned it over, and peeled off the papery hull to study it. "So the fasting is over now? Just like that?"

Owen decided to test what he actually knew. "The whole month was called Ramadan," he said. "We fasted from dawn until sunset, every day of it. Today is Eid al-Fitr, the celebration that marks the end. So this morning nobody at my house got up before sunrise. My dad slept in for the first time in a month." He watched his uncle at the far table, working through a plate of sheer khurma at a pace that suggested a man making up for lost time, and the pieces fit together in his head. The hunger had been the point of the month, and the feast was the point of its ending.

"Then I messed up," Demi said, staring at his untouched bowl. "I skipped breakfast for nothing."

Owen slid the bowl closer. "You accidentally did Ramadan for one morning. That's one more than me. I ate a whole bagel at seven."

His uncle leaned over from the next table, nodding at Demi with something close to respect. "MashaAllah, the boy kept a fast on Eid. Now he must consume double to break it properly." Demi picked up the spoon, and Owen's aunt was already heading back with a second helping.

activity: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
knowledge_domain: to read the rights listed in their country's constitution or charter and explain one in their own words
fact: The Canadian Charter applies to governments and their actions, not directly to private businesses or individuals.
story:
Evan stood in the lobby of city hall with his class, holding his cue cards so tightly that the corners bent. In twenty minutes, each student had to stand up in the council chamber and explain one right from the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms in their own words, and Evan was still not sure his was right.

"It's the backpack thing," he told Zach, who was practising freedom of expression into his phone's voice recorder. "The convenience store near my house put up a sign saying no backpacks allowed. I wanted to do my explanation on that, how the store broke the Charter."

Zach lowered his phone. "Broke it? Stores can do that?"

"Let's test it," Evan said. He found Yassine by the display of municipal bylaws and laid out his idea like an experiment. "The Charter protects freedom, right? A rule against backpacks restricts what I can carry, so it should be a Charter problem. But watch this." He pointed at the bylaw display, then at the room around them. "Everything here belongs to the government. The council chamber, the bylaws, the security guard at the desk. The Charter is about this stuff. The store isn't any of this. The store is private."

Yassine frowned, then nodded slowly. "So the Charter applies to governments and their actions, not to a private business."

"That's what I think. But I could be wrong," Evan admitted. He looked around for their teacher. "Ms. Aziz, if the government banned backpacks in this building, would that be a Charter issue, but if my corner store does it, it isn't?"

Ms. Aziz smiled. "You've noticed something real, Evan. Try it out loud and see how it lands."

When his turn came, Evan walked to the front of the chamber, his voice steadier with each sentence. "My right is freedom against unreasonable search. The Charter covers what governments do. If a government official searched my backpack for no reason, that could violate the Charter. But if a store owner asks me to leave my backpack at the counter, that's a private rule, more like the store setting conditions for coming in." He paused. "At first I thought the store was being unfair, even biased against teenagers. That might still be true, and there are other laws about that. It just isn't a Charter thing, because the Charter applies to governments and their actions, not directly to private businesses or individuals."

Afterward, Ms. Aziz suggested he revise one sentence to make the distinction sharper, and he sat on the chamber's front step scribbling the new wording while Zach read his cue cards over his shoulder. Yassine flopped down beside them and said, "So tomorrow we ask the store owner why the sign went up, and see if it's even a real rule."

Evan clicked his pen. "Field trip number two."

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In the United States, the cost of crude oil is usually the largest single part of the price of a gallon of gasoline, so pump prices tend to rise when crude oil prices rise.
story:
The number on the sign had changed again. Adam stood beside his dad's car at the gas station, staring up at the tall white board where the price of regular read forty cents more than it had last Saturday. He had been saving his allowance for a new bike lock, and every dollar his dad spent on gas felt like a dollar that might not show up as allowance next week. That was the real problem. Adam wanted to know if this was temporary or if gas was going to eat the bike lock forever.

Beside pump three, a kid about his age was tugging his mother's sleeve. "Mom, why is it more than last week? Did the gas station people just decide to be mean?" She shrugged and kept cleaning her sunglasses. Adam wandered over. "I heard my dad say crude oil went up," he offered. The kid, whose name turned out to be Domenico, squinted at him. "Crude oil? What's that got to do with the pump?"

That was the question Adam couldn't quite answer. He knew crude oil was the stuff from the ground, and gasoline came from it somehow, but how much did the oil matter compared to everything else? There was a small TV inside the gas station, mounted above the coffee machine, and through the window Adam could see a financial channel with a red arrow climbing beside the words CRUDE OIL. He made a diagnosis of the situation, or tried to: if the oil part got more expensive, the gas got more expensive. But how big was the oil part? Was it a sliver of the price or the biggest chunk of it?

He tested it. First he asked the cashier if the station had raised its own prices. "Nah, man, we don't decide that," the cashier said, sliding a hot dog roller into place. "Biggest single part of every gallon is the crude oil itself. When crude goes up, our pump price goes up." Adam filed that away. So the hidden cause wasn't the station being mean, and it wasn't some tiny detail either. The oil was the largest single piece of the gallon, sitting under the price like the bottom block in a tower.

Back outside, Domenico was waiting by the ice machine with his friend Jaiveer, who had been nominated by their soccer team that morning to pick up the orange slices and was now counting quarters at the counter. "So?" Domenico said. "Did you solve the mystery?" Adam pointed at the TV through the glass. "Crude oil prices went up, and crude oil is usually the biggest single part of a gallon of gas, so the pump price follows it. When oil goes back down, the pump should too." Domenico looked from the screen to the sign, like he was watching two ends of the same rope.

"Then it's not permanent," Adam said, mostly to himself, and the tight feeling about the bike lock loosened a little. His dad finished filling the tank and waved him over. As they pulled out of the station, Adam turned in his seat to watch the big white sign shrink behind them, and he wondered whether the number on it would be lower next Saturday, and whether somewhere far away the price of oil was already falling. "Hey, Dad," he said, "can we drive past here again next weekend?"

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: Masaccio's Holy Trinity fresco in Florence, painted around 1427, is one of the earliest paintings built on a single vanishing point.
story:
Carson slumped in the third row of Ms. Tang's art room, staring at a blank page. The assignment on the board said "Street, one-point perspective," and everyone else was already drawing.

"You just draw the road first," Taha whispered, sliding his sketch across the table. "Big V in the middle."

Carson tried it. His road looked like a slice of arid desert, flat and dead, nothing like a street. He erased it so hard the paper tore a little, which embarrassed him even though nobody laughed. He tried again. Two curbs, a horizon line, still wrong. The buildings leaned like tired old men.

At lunch he found Philippe in the library with a printout of an old painting, a vaulted ceiling arching over three figures. "It's from Florence," Philippe said. "Masaccio's Holy Trinity fresco, painted around 1427." He ran his finger along the edge of the painted ceiling, one beam, then another, then the floor lines. "Watch. They all head somewhere."

Carson grabbed a ruler from his backpack. He lined it up with one ceiling edge and drew the extension lightly in pencil across the whole print. Then he did the next one. The lines crossed at a single point behind the standing figures. Every one of them. He tried the floor lines next, and they hit the same spot.

"One point," Carson said. "Everything goes to one point. That's the whole trick." He felt the insight land like a door swinging open. If the fresco's lines all obeyed one spot, his street could too. He copied the printout and dashed back to the art room, asking Ms. Tang if he could work through lunch. She raised an eyebrow and handed him a fresh sheet.

He drew a horizon first this time, then marked a dot in the middle of it with a hard press of the pencil. The curbs started at the bottom corners and ran straight to the dot. So did the rooflines, the shop windows, the cracks in the sidewalk. The buildings stood up straight at last, because their side edges angled toward that same point.

By the end of the period Taha leaned over, squinting at the page. "It looks like a real street," he said. "How'd you figure that out?"

Carson tapped the dot at the center of the horizon with his ruler. "Six hundred years before us, some guy in Florence already figured it out," he said. "I just followed his lines."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: The forearm has two bones: the radius, on the thumb side, and the ulna, on the little-finger side.
story:
Ava sat on the paper-covered bed in the emergency room, holding her right arm against her chest like a bird with a folded wing. It had happened at the skate park: one moment she was airborne off the quarter pipe, the next she was on the ramp with her wrist bent underneath her. The pain was a bright, humming thing, and the smell of antiseptic made her stomach lurch every time a nurse walked past.

"You're in the broken-bone category now," said Markus, who had ridden in the ambulance with her because his mom worked at the hospital and knew the shortcut. "Congrats. It's the coolest category."

"It's not cool, it's purple," Ava said, looking at the swelling above her wrist. The doctor had come and gone, ordered an X-ray, and left the films clipped to a light box by the sink. Ava stared at them while they waited. Two pale stripes ran down the middle of her forearm, side by side, and one of them had a thin dark crack in it, like a hairline in a windshield.

"Which one is it?" Markus asked, squinting. "There's two."

Ava pointed her left index finger at the films and then, slowly, held up her uninjured left hand, palm out. She put her thumb on one side and her pinky on the other and imagined them wrapping down her own forearm to the wrist. The thumb-side bone would line up with one stripe, the little-finger-side with the other. She traced the cracked stripe down toward the hand and saw it landed, when she held her palm forward, on the thumb side. "This one," she said, tapping the film. "The thumb-side one."

"The what?" said Xander, arriving breathless with her backpack and a chocolate milk from the vending machine, which he now looked ashamed of.

"The forearm has two bones," Ava said. "The radius is the thumb side, and the ulna is the little-finger side."

Xander looked skeptical. "You made that up just now."

"I tested it. Thumb side, cracked stripe. Same side."

When the doctor came back in, Markus made Ava recount her whole method, thumbs and pinkies and stripes, and the doctor looked at the film and then at her. "Radius," he confirmed. "Nondisplaced fracture. Nice detective work." Ava grinned so wide the pain in her arm almost didn't register.

By the time the cast was on, a stiff blue shell from wrist to elbow, Ava had already decided on a plan. She would learn every fall from her coach, wear the wrist guards she had been too stubborn to use, and be back at the park by August. "Sign it," she said, holding the cast out to Markus and the marker like it was a cast album. Xander uncapped his pen and wrote his name crooked down the middle.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: Simmering a sauce with the lid off lets water escape as steam, so the sauce slowly gets thicker.
story:
Alexa's dad had left a note on the fridge: back at seven, dinner is yours. Below it sat two onions, a can of tomatoes, and a dusty recipe card from her grandmother. Alexa wanted to make the sauce herself, all of it, because last week she had burned instant noodles and Dimitri had not let it go since. She called Mr. Tan, the neighbour across the hall, who had once been a cook.

"The claw grip," he said, holding up his own hand. "Fingers curled under, knuckles forward. The blade rides the knuckles, and it can't get your fingertips." He watched her curl her hand over the onion like a small angry paw. "Good. Now the dice for soup is bigger, but for sauce you want it fine." She cut slowly, and only cried a little, and Mr. Tan said the tears were normal and not a failure.

Mr. Tan left for his evening walk, and Alexa carried the pot to the stove alone. The recipe card said simmer for forty minutes, and she set the timer and clapped the lid on so nothing would splash. While it burbled, she texted Dimitri a photo of her chopped onion. He replied that his microwave was not obsolete, actually, and that real cooking was a scam invented by commerce, which she decided was a compliment.

At forty minutes she lifted the lid and stirred. The sauce was thin, more like soup, and dinner was in twenty minutes. She checked the card again, then stood still and thought. Steam was water leaving the pot, and water had to go somewhere. With the lid on, it hit the lid, cooled, and dripped back in. She had kept the water prisoner. She slid the lid half off, then thought again and took it off completely, and turned the heat up a little.

Fifteen minutes later Dimitri and Lucie arrived, because she had promised them pasta. Lucie leaned over the pot. "It's actually thick," she said. "How?"

"Simmering with the lid off lets water escape as steam, so the sauce gets thicker," Alexa said. "I had the lid on the whole time before that."

"Show me the onion thing," Dimitri said, and pulled a knife from the block without asking. Alexa put out a cutting board, curled her hand into a claw, and slid the onion toward him.

activity: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
knowledge_domain: to measure the speed of a rolling ball from distance and time and draw a distance-time graph
fact: On a distance-time graph, a straight sloping line means the object is moving at a constant speed.
story:
Grayson crouched at the top of the playground ramp with a tennis ball in one hand and his phone in the other, wondering whether the ball would slow down on the way to the fence or keep going the same the whole time. He had promised his tutor, Mr. Ong, that he would finish his graphing homework before Saturday, but the assignment felt flat on paper. Speed from distance and time, that was all it was, so he had decided to measure it for real. Syeda stood by the fence with a stopwatch, and Keon waited halfway down with a stick to mark where the ball passed each second.

"Ready?" Syeda called. "Say go."

Grayson let the ball roll. It hissed over the rubber matting, wobbled once where a crack crossed the ramp, and kept going. Keon dropped his stick flat the instant the ball passed his feet, then jumped back to avoid it. Syeda clicked the stopwatch and shouted the time, and Grayson scrawled the numbers in his notebook: one second, two metres; two seconds, four metres; three seconds, six.

"Again," he said. "Same ramp, same push. If it's the same, then it's not luck."

They ran it four more times. On the fourth try a pigeon wandered across the path and nearly hindered the whole experiment, but the ball curved around it and still reached the fence in six seconds. When Grayson plotted every run on his distance-time graph, he sat back on his heels. All the points lay along one clean, straight line, climbing from the bottom left corner to the top right. He had expected a curve, some sign of the ball tiring out.

"Look at this," he said, holding the notebook up. "I thought it would bend."

Syeda leaned in and frowned at the page. "It's just... straight. That's kind of radical, honestly. Like the ball refuses to slow down."

"It means it's moving at a constant speed," Grayson said slowly, tracing the slope with his finger. Every metre took the same amount of time, from the first second to the last, and the straight sloping line was telling him that without a single word. He checked the fence, then the ramp, then the line again, and a wondering question crept into his head: would the line stay straight if the surface were rougher? If it bent, where would it bend first, the start or the end?

They found the patch of gravel near the swings. Grayson crouched again, ball in hand, notebook open to a fresh page. "Keon, grab your stick," he said. "New ground, same push."

Keon ran for the stick, and Syeda reset the stopwatch to zero.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Cortisol is a hormone made by the adrenal glands that rises during stress; when stress lasts a long time, cortisol can stay high.
story:
Kate was doing homework on Thursday when her phone started buzzing like a trapped hornet. The group chat, the one named "Casserole Club" because Cassius had misspelled "Cassius's Club" once and it stuck, had gone from zero messages to forty in three minutes. She scrolled up. Hayley had posted "does anyone else feel like their brain is a browser with 900 tabs open" at 4:02, then "sorry ignore that" at 4:02 and one second, then a photo of her volleyball schedule, which had been compressed this season into something with no white space left on it.

Kate read the whole thing twice. It wasn't just tonight. Going back through the chat, Hayley's messages turned sharp on Sunday evenings, droopy on Wednesdays, and once she'd posted a picture of a tropical beach with the caption "take me," which was not like her, since Hayley hated sand. Kate thought about it the way she thought about math problems, looking for the pattern instead of the noise. The noise was volleyball. The pattern was that Hayley had been worried about tryouts since the first week of school, and tryouts were over, and the worry hadn't stopped. Something was staying on.

"Can I call you for a sec," she typed, and then did before anyone could answer no.

The next day Hayley came to school with a printout from a doctor's visit her mom had made her go to, because she'd been tired for weeks and getting every cold that circulated. "Okay so listen," Hayley said at lunch, flattening the paper on the table like it was evidence. "There's this hormone called cortisol. It's made by the adrenal glands, and it rises during stress. And the doctor said when stress lasts a long time, cortisol can stay high. That's why I feel like a phone at two percent." She paused. "Also she said the word anxiety out loud, which was weirdly a relief."

"So it's not that you're broken," Kate said. "It's that your alarm's been going off since September."

"Basically. She called it stress that never got the memo to stop."

Cassius, who had been eating fries through all of this, held one up. "So what's the coping plan? Not to be rude, but you snapped at me about a pencil on Tuesday and I still have feelings."

The plan they worked out in the group chat that night was simpler than Kate expected: Hayley would tell Coach she needed Sundays off, which the doctor had called setting boundaries, and Kate would stop forwarding her every meme about tropical vacations at midnight. Kate tested it quietly, watching the chat like an experiment. Sunday night came and went. No sharp messages. On Wednesday Hayley posted a photo of her homework, finished, with the caption "look at her go."

Cassius replied with a fry emoji and the words, "Is she under warranty? Asking for the club."

"Out of warranty," Hayley typed back. "Running on pure cortisol and spite."
